say.text: After Shirkuh's death, some of the emirs whom Nur ad-Din had sent to Egypt aspired to the command of the whole army and to the vizierate. Ibn al-Athir names four.
Ain ad-Dawla al-Yaruqi, the chief among them, who had the most troops.
Qutb ad-Din Khusraw ibn Talil, a nephew of the emir Abu'l-Hayja, once lord of Arbela.
Sayf ad-Din Ali ibn Ahmad al-Hakkari, called al-Mashtub, 'the scarred', whose grandfather had held castles in the Hakkari country.
And Shihab ad-Din Mahmud al-Harimi, one of Salah ad-Din's maternal uncles. Each had gathered his troops, and meant to seize the power by force.

The caliph al-Adid then sent for Salah ad-Din, to invest him as vizier in place of his uncle. He thought that a man with no troops and no party would be easy to rule, and meant to win over part of the Syrian army and send the rest out of the country.
Salah ad-Din refused at first, shrinking from so high a place. Pressed, he accepted, much against his will.
At the palace he was given the robe of the vizier, the turban and the other emblems of the office, and the title al-Malik an-Nasir, 'the helping king'. Then he went back to the house of Shirkuh.
None of the emirs who had hoped for the power came to pay him the slightest respect.
Isa al-Hakkari, a jurist, who had stayed at his side, set out to win the emirs over, one by one.
They will not come to you, my lord, because they have each been promised something, or hope to be. They will come to someone who shows them what they stand to lose.
I would rather they came because they believed in the cause.
Then you will have three men. I will bring you the others. Give me the camp and the days.
